title: When Money Stopped Being Believed
subtitle: The German hyperinflation and the Rentenmark, Berlin, Dresden, Hamburg and the Rhine, 1922–1923
intro: In July 1914 a dollar bought 4.20 marks. On 20 November 1923 it bought 4.2 trillion, and on that day the German authorities stopped the fall by declaring that one new Rentenmark would equal one trillion old paper marks. Nothing physical had changed overnight. The presses had been ordered to stop and a new unit was offered, backed on paper by a mortgage on German land and industry rather than by gold, and enough people agreed to accept it. This chapter lays side by side the people who watched the old agreement die and the people who wrote the new one.

The fall is measured in the official record: about 9,000 marks to the dollar in November 1922; around 21,000 through the spring of 1923, when the Reichsbank briefly propped the rate; over a million by the end of July; 160 million by the end of September, after the government ended passive resistance in the Ruhr; and past a trillion on 14 November. Inside those numbers are the dated voices. In Berlin, Käthe Kollwitz's diary records the intellectual middle class being wiped out and a loaf of bread at 140 billion. Betty Scholem, who ran a family printing works, wrote to her son in Jerusalem that postage would double in two days. A man known only as Wolfgang wrote to an American composer that the pensioners in his building were starving. In Dresden, Victor Klemperer watched the price of his wife's coffee double while she drank it. Harry Graf Kessler compared the daily dollar rate to a fever chart.

Around them stand the people who saw it from outside or from above. Ernest Hemingway, aged 23, crossed the Rhine from Strasbourg to Kehl in September 1922 and wrote for Toronto readers how ten francs bought a feast, and how an old man could not afford the apples. Lord D'Abernon, the British ambassador, kept a diary in Berlin that he published in 1929. Hjalmar Schacht, appointed currency commissioner on 12 November 1923, wrote his own account in 1927. Two later voices are labelled as later: Erna von Pustau of Hamburg, whose memories Pearl Buck published in 1947, and Edgar Bissantz, an American student who closed his father's Bremen account in 1923 and wrote about it in 1986.

The French and Belgian side appears only as context. Their troops entered the Ruhr on 11 January 1923 to enforce reparations deliveries, and the German government answered with paid passive resistance, financed by printing money. No French or Belgian diaries are included here. Other gaps: no industrial worker's or farmer's diary was found in a form that could be verified; Reichsbank president Rudolf Havenstein, who died on 20 November 1923, left official statements but no diary used here; no New York Times dispatch could be reached; and Adam Fergusson's 1975 compilation 'When Money Dies' is not used as a source. Where possible the underlying diaries are cited directly.

Much of the record is letters, newspaper dispatches, an economic weekly and official decrees, not diaries, and the form tags say so. The hardship is set out soberly. In the autumn of 1923 hunger turned into looting, and on 5 November a crowd attacked the Jewish residents of Berlin's Scheunenviertel. Kollwitz recorded attempted pogroms, and Erna von Pustau later remembered how people in her circle blamed Jews for the inflation. Those accusations appear here only as things the sources recorded, and they are not repeated.
calendar_note: All dates are Gregorian. German usage needs care: German 'Milliarde' is the English (short-scale) billion (10^9), and German 'Billion' is the English trillion (10^12). The figures here use English short-scale words: the Rentenmark equalled one trillion (eine Billion) paper marks. Dollar rates differ between sources because some give month-end rates, some monthly averages and some a single day's quotation; the date of each figure is given wherever it is known. Several diary entries are known only to the month from the excerpts available, and they are marked 'approx'.
seam: These records treat money as something that exists only while people agree to take it. Hemingway's old man, Wolfgang's starving pensioners and Kollwitz's ruined middle class were the people who still believed in the paper while others had stopped. Then the agreement was remade: a decree, a commissioner, a mortgage on land and a fixed rate, and by December Kessler saw shoppers back in the food shops. As in Omelas, the new calm rested on losses no one repaid. The savings wiped out in 1923 were never restored.

eyes.name: Ernest Miller Hemingway
eyes.role: Aged 23; European correspondent of the Toronto Daily Star and Star Weekly, based in Paris
eyes.where: Paris; trips into Germany, including Strasbourg to Kehl across the Rhine, summer 1922
eyes.authenticity: Published in the Toronto Daily Star and Toronto Star Weekly in 1922; reprinted in later collections (Dateline: Toronto) and excerpted by German History in Documents and Images (GHDI). The 1 September piece is titled 'Germans are Doggedly Sullen or Desperate Over the Mark', not 'Doggedly Sure'.
eyes.bio: Before his first novel, Hemingway was a newspaperman paid by the piece. His 1922 inflation stories turn the exchange rate into the prices of things: a lunch, a slice of cake, a few apples. They show how a currency collapse made foreigners rich at the border and left the local poor behind.

eyes.name: Käthe Kollwitz
eyes.role: Graphic artist and sculptor, aged 55–56; wife of the panel doctor Karl Kollwitz; mother of Peter, killed in October 1914
eyes.where: Weißenburger Straße, Prenzlauer Berg, a working-class district of north Berlin
eyes.vantage_label: artist in a poor Berlin district
eyes.authenticity: Her diary was kept from 1908 to 1943. Selections were published in 1948 (Tagebuchblätter und Briefe) and in English in 1955; the full edition is Die Tagebücher, ed. Jutta Bohnke-Kollwitz (Siedler, 1989). The entries here follow the GHDI translation from that edition. Copyrighted: summaries only.
eyes.bio: Kollwitz lived among the patients of her husband's working-class practice, and in 1923 she was making woodcuts on hunger. Her diary sets the dollar rate beside family grief and street scenes. It also records the small, odd details that show the strain, like a toddler asking how the dollar is doing.

sources.title: Käthe Kollwitz on the Hyperinflation (1922–23), GHDI

eyes.name: Harry Graf Kessler
eyes.role: Diplomat, publisher and patron of modern art, aged 54–55; left-liberal (DDP) and pacifist
eyes.authenticity: Kessler kept a diary from 1880 to 1937. It is published in full in the Cotta edition (Das Tagebuch 1880–1937) and in English selection as Berlin in Lights (trans. Charles Kessler). The 1922 and 1923 entries here are known from Volker Ullrich's quotation of them (bpb, 2023); exact days are not given there. Copyrighted: summary and a phrase only.
eyes.bio: Kessler knew almost everyone in politics and the arts, and his diary has long served historians as a record of Weimar Berlin. His 1923 entries read the exchange rate like a doctor reading a chart. He saw the Rentenmark winter as the first light after a long dark.

sources.title: Volker Ullrich, '1923 als Schlüsseljahr für 1933?', APuZ / bpb (2023)

eyes.name: Victor Klemperer
eyes.role: Professor of Romance languages at the Technische Hochschule Dresden, aged 41–42; of Jewish birth, converted to Protestantism; married to the pianist Eva Klemperer
eyes.vantage_label: salaried professor watching his savings vanish
eyes.authenticity: The 1918–1924 diaries were published as Leben sammeln, nicht fragen wozu und warum (Aufbau, 1996). The entries here are known from quotations by Volker Ullrich (bpb, 2023) and Richard J. Evans (The Coming of the Third Reich, 2003, p. 107). Copyrighted: summaries only.
eyes.bio: Klemperer is best known for his diaries of the Nazi years, but he was already writing everything down in 1923. His entries put the inflation into a professor's household budget: coffee, salary, insurance and food. He also recorded his fear as a Jew when the crisis turned ugly.

sources.title: Facing History, 'When Money Had No Value' (Klemperer excerpt via Evans)

eyes.name: Betty Scholem (née Hirsch)
eyes.role: Aged 57; widow of Arthur Scholem, co-running the family printing firm in Berlin with her sons; mother of Gershom Scholem
eyes.authenticity: Her letters to Gershom, who had emigrated to Palestine in September 1923, are published in Mutter und Sohn im Briefwechsel 1917–1946 (C.H. Beck, 1989) and in English in Gershom Scholem, A Life in Letters (Harvard, 2002); excerpted by GHDI. Copyrighted: summaries only.
eyes.bio: Betty Scholem's letters show the inflation from inside a business with a payroll. The printing firm turned itself into a money-handling operation, buying dollars to protect wages. Every letter gives its own cost of postage, which shows how quickly prices were moving.

eyes.name: 'Wolfgang' (surname not given)
eyes.role: A Berlin resident writing to the American composer Edgar Stillman Kelley; probably a former student; working on illustrations or models for Kelley's 'Pilgrim's Progress'
eyes.authenticity: Originals in the Edgar Stillman Kelley Collection, Western College Memorial Archives, Oxford, Ohio (Box 17, Letters 1922–1924); English translation by Ellen Yutzy Glebe for GHDI. Only his first name appears in the published edition.
eyes.bio: Wolfgang is the least prominent voice here. He was asking an American patron for work and an invitation abroad. His letters change a ten-dollar cheque into the price of milk, and they note that an elderly neighbour on a small pension died almost every week.

sources.title: Letters to America Reflect the Effects of Hyperinflation in Berlin (February 1923), GHDI

eyes.name: Edgar Vincent, 1st Viscount D'Abernon
eyes.role: British ambassador in Berlin 1920–1926, aged 65–66; a former financier and Ottoman debt administrator
eyes.vantage_label: foreign ambassador with a banker's eye
eyes.authenticity: Published as An Ambassador of Peace (Hodder and Stoughton, 3 vols., 1929–1930); vol. II, covering 1922–1923, appeared in 1929. The published diary was selected and annotated, so it is not a raw manuscript. Because it was first published after 1928 it is summarised here; the dated entries are known from Ullrich (bpb, 2023). He also lectured on the subject in 'German Currency: Its Collapse and Recovery, 1920–26' (Royal Statistical Society, 1926).
eyes.bio: D'Abernon had run the finances of Egypt and the Ottoman public debt, so he saw a currency collapse as a professional matter. His diary records the Ruhr crisis and the year's end with an ambassador's sense of how near Germany came to the edge. He was among the British officials who favoured stabilisation over punishment.

sources.title: An Ambassador of Peace (1929), HathiTrust record
German Currency: Its Collapse and Recovery, 1920–6 (1926), HathiTrust record

eyes.name: Hjalmar Horace Greeley Schacht
eyes.role: Banker (Darmstädter und Nationalbank), aged 46; appointed Reich Currency Commissioner on 12 November 1923, Reichsbank president from December 1923
eyes.vantage_label: the commissioner who held the new line
eyes.authenticity: Die Stabilisierung der Mark (Deutsche Verlags-Anstalt, 1927); English as The Stabilization of the Mark (New York: Adelphi; London: Allen & Unwin, 1927). It is his own account, written four years later, when he wanted credit for the stabilisation. Published before 1929, so it may be quoted.
eyes.bio: Schacht was brought in to defend the Rentenmark. His task was to stop new paper money and hold the rate long enough for people to believe in it. His 1927 book is an insider's justification and should be read as one. His later career as Hitler's Reichsbank president and economics minister lies outside this chapter.

sources.title: Hjalmar Schacht on the Stabilization of the Mark (1927), GHDI

eyes.name: Reich government and Reichsbank (official record)
eyes.role: Decrees, cabinet decisions and official exchange quotations of the German Reich and its central bank
eyes.authenticity: Dates and rates as given by Volker Ullrich (bpb, 2023), the Deutsches Historisches Museum (LeMO) and the Reichsbank figures reproduced there. Month-end rates and monthly averages differ between sources.
eyes.bio: Behind every price in the diaries is the official sequence of decisions: paying for passive resistance, propping and then dropping the rate, the Rentenbank decree, the stop to printing, and the fixed conversion. These are the records of the agreement itself.

eyes.name: Wirtschaftsdienst (Hamburg economic weekly)
eyes.role: Weekly of the Hamburg World Economic Archive (HWWA); the 2 November 1923 article's author is illegible in the scan
eyes.authenticity: Wirtschaftsdienst no. 44, 2 November 1923, pp. 1005–1006, digitised by the journal's 'Vor 100 Jahren' series. Byline partly illegible.
eyes.bio: A professional journal writing during the changeover, before anyone knew whether the Rentenmark would hold. It sets out the improvised mix of money then in use: local emergency notes, dollar certificates, gold-loan notes. It saw that the whole transition would turn on whether people accepted the new unit at face value.

eyes.name: Erna von Pustau
eyes.role: Youngest of three daughters of a Hamburg merchant family, a young woman in 1923; emigrated to New York in the early 1940s
eyes.vantage_label: daughter of a ruined merchant family (remembered later)
eyes.form: memoir (written later, as told to Pearl S. Buck)
eyes.authenticity: Her recollections appear in Pearl S. Buck, How It Happens: Talk About the German People, 1914–1933, with Erna von Pustau (John Day, 1947). They are memories recorded about 24 years later through another writer's editing, so they are labelled later firsthand. Known here through a 2022 Financial History article. Summary only.
eyes.bio: Von Pustau's account explains what the inflation did to belief as well as to bank balances. She remembered her own father, once a respected merchant, taking up the scapegoating of Jews that the crisis fed. The record shows that the false explanations spread along with the losses.

eyes.name: Edgar Bissantz
eyes.role: American student on a European tour in 1923; later an architect in Santa Barbara, California
eyes.vantage_label: American visitor closing a dead account (remembered later)
eyes.authenticity: 'Memories of the 1923 German Inflation', The Freeman / FEE, 1 September 1986. Written about 63 years after the event. Copyrighted: summary only.
eyes.bio: Bissantz's father had followed a Wichita banker's advice and put a thousand dollars into marks in a Bremen bank. His story follows a foreign saver's money down to nothing. The ending is as plain as the rest: the postage cost more than what was left in the account.

sources.title: Edgar Bissantz, 'Memories of the 1923 German Inflation' (FEE, 1986)

entries.headline: A German export tax catches the 'exchange pirates'
entries.digest: Months before the hyperinflation proper, the Star Weekly ran Hemingway's piece headlined 'Exchange Pirates Hit by German Export Tax'. Its subject was foreigners who used strong currencies to buy cheaply in Germany. It shows that a falling mark was already drawing bargain-hunters across the border in early 1922.
entries.source_note: Title, paper and date as listed by GHDI ('Ernest Hemingway: Inflation Stories'); the content summary rests on the title and GHDI's framing, not a full reading.

entries.headline: Germans watch their currency plunge, each by temperament
entries.digest: Hemingway described Germans watching the mark fall: some doggedly sullen, some desperate. He pointed to Austria, where the crown had gone from 800 to 22,000 to the dollar, and explained that German newspapers now printed the daily mark rate in large type on their front pages. The exchange rate had become the main news.
entries.quote: The German people, according to their temperaments, are watching the plunge to worthlessness of their currency
entries.source_note: 'Germans are Doggedly Sullen or Desperate Over the Mark', Toronto Daily Star, 1 September 1922; text via GHDI.

entries.headline: Ten francs across the Rhine buys a pocketful of marks
entries.digest: Changing money in Strasbourg before crossing the bridge to Kehl, Hemingway got 670 marks for ten francs, about ninety Canadian cents. At 800 marks to the dollar, Kehl's best hotel served a five-course set lunch for 120 marks, about fifteen cents, and cake shops sold cream-filled slices at five marks. Crowds came over from the French side to eat and buy cheaply.
entries.quote: For ten francs I received 670 marks.
entries.source_note: 'Crossing to Germany: A Way to Make Money', Toronto Daily Star, 19 September 1922; text via GHDI. The trip itself took place shortly before publication; its exact day is not given.

entries.headline: An old man cannot afford the apples
entries.digest: A white-bearded gentleman who had watched Hemingway buy apples asked their price. Told twelve marks, less than two cents to a visitor, he said he could not pay it and walked away, still looking at the fruit. Hemingway's point was that pensioners and others on fixed incomes, such as holders of war bonds, could not keep up as the mark fell.
entries.quote: I can't pay it. It is too much.
entries.source_note: Same article, Toronto Daily Star, 19 September 1922; GHDI.

entries.headline: The dollar rate reads like a fever chart
entries.digest: With the dollar at about 9,000 marks, Kessler wrote that the daily rate showed the country's decline the way a fever chart shows a gravely ill patient's. For him the exchange rate had become a measure of the nation's health as well as a price.
entries.source_note: Quoted (German) by Ullrich, bpb 2023, as early November 1922; exact day not given there.

entries.headline: The dollar stands near 9,000 marks
entries.digest: By November 1922 the dollar cost about 9,000 marks, roughly two thousand times its 1914 price of 4.20. In Berlin, new joint-stock companies were being founded in large numbers as people turned money into anything that might hold value.
entries.source_note: Rate: Ullrich, bpb 2023. Berliner Zeitung (2023) cites the Frankfurter Zeitung for 468 new companies in Berlin that month.

entries.headline: A dark year-end: the intellectual middle class is being wiped out
entries.digest: Kollwitz ended 1922 in gloom. Germany was in a bad way, she wrote, and its intellectual middle class was being wiped out. She copied a bitter children's Christmas verse from Simplicissimus, about bread, beer, a drinking father and a hungry child, and answered it with sarcasm.
entries.source_note: Die Tagebücher (1989), pp. 543–44; GHDI translation.

entries.headline: French and Belgian troops occupy the Ruhr
entries.digest: French and Belgian troops entered the Ruhr, Germany's coal and steel heartland, to enforce reparations deliveries the Reparations Commission had declared in default. Berlin answered with passive resistance and paid idle workers and firms with newly printed money, which broke what was left of the mark. (French and Belgian records are context only in this chapter.)
entries.source_note: Date: Ullrich, bpb 2023; GHDI abstract to document 5414.

entries.headline: A patriotic wave sweeps class hatred away
entries.digest: In the first weeks of the occupation D'Abernon noted that the French entry had done what nothing else could. Class hatred seemed swept away by a wave of patriotic feeling, and the country looked united behind resistance. He wrote as someone who doubted how long that unity, and the money paying for it, could last.
entries.source_note: An Ambassador of Peace, vol. II (1929), as quoted by Ullrich, bpb 2023; exact day not given there. The final sentence is a general characterisation of his stance.

entries.headline: A ten-dollar cheque is worth three-fifty; milk is 560 marks
entries.digest: Wolfgang thanked Kelley for a registered letter and a ten-dollar cheque, then explained it had shrunk to about $3.50 in local purchasing power, largely since the Ruhr occupation. Milk cost 560 marks a litre. Elderly people on small pensions in his building were starving, and someone died almost every week. A job offered three months earlier had vanished when the firm closed its office, and he asked to be invited to Ohio.
entries.source_note: Edgar Stillman Kelley Collection, Western College Memorial Archives, Box 17; GHDI document 5414.

entries.headline: Prices in cents: the city has gone mad
entries.digest: At 19,000 marks to the dollar, Wolfgang turned a newspaper's price list into American money: meat 15–18 cents a pound, an egg 2 cents, a loaf 20 cents, coal 45 cents a hundredweight. To a dollar-holder Germany was cheap, and to a mark-earner the same prices were impossible. He called Berlin completely insane.
entries.source_note: Kelley Collection; GHDI document 5414.

entries.headline: Shoppers stop buying, waiting for the dollar
entries.digest: Wolfgang enclosed a Mittagszeitung article on price cuts. It reported trade almost at a standstill: even the rich and the foreigners had stopped buying. Shoes cost 60,000–120,000 marks, a cooking pot 30,000, and some tailors priced imported cloth in sterling. Sellers and speculators fed the fear that the dollar would rise again.
entries.source_note: Mittagszeitung, 17 February 1923, enclosed in the letter of that date; GHDI document 5414.

entries.headline: A pause: the Reichsbank holds the dollar near 21,000
entries.digest: For about three months the Reichsbank sold foreign exchange and gold to hold the dollar at roughly 21,000 marks. The pause could not last while passive resistance in the Ruhr was still paid for with new money.
entries.source_note: Ullrich, bpb 2023 (rate 'about 21,000', February–April). Smithsonian (2023) gives 17,000 for January and 24,000 for April as monthly figures.

entries.headline: Closing a thousand dollars' worth of marks
entries.digest: In 1923 the Bremen bank asked the student's father to withdraw his balance. On a Wichita banker's advice he had bought $1,000 of marks, and statements had shown it eaten away by postage, fees and inflation. Bissantz closed the account and received a few almost worthless notes. At the post office the postage to send them home cost more than the notes were worth, and the clerk pencilled the amount on the envelope.
entries.source_note: FEE, 1 September 1986. Season and exact date not given in the text.

entries.headline: The middle class loses its fortune and looks for someone to blame
entries.digest: Von Pustau remembered how the middle class, having lost its fortunes, became open to antisemitic propaganda. In her circle 'stock exchange' and 'Jews' were run together in people's minds, and Jews were blamed for the inflation. Her account records this scapegoating as a historical fact about how the crisis was explained, and it is reported here only for that reason.
entries.form: memoir (as told to Pearl S. Buck, 1947)
entries.source_note: Buck, How It Happens (1947), via Financial History 142 (2022), p. 36.

entries.headline: The dollar passes a million marks
entries.digest: By the end of July the dollar cost more than a million paper marks, fifty times its spring level. Employers began paying wages daily and then twice a day, and people spent them at once.
entries.source_note: Rate: Ullrich, bpb 2023. The wage practice is a general description drawn from GHDI and Smithsonian summaries, not a single dated document.

entries.headline: The coffee doubles in price while it is drunk
entries.digest: Klemperer's wife ordered a coffee at a station. The price board showed 6,000 marks, but by the time she had finished, the waiter wanted 12,000 and the posted price had been changed. The diary records it plainly as a fact of the week.
entries.source_note: Leben sammeln (1996), quoted (German) by Ullrich, bpb 2023, as early August 1923.

entries.headline: Cuno falls; Stresemann takes over with the dollar at 3.7 million
entries.digest: Chancellor Wilhelm Cuno resigned and Gustav Stresemann formed a grand coalition, with the dollar at about 3.7 million marks. The Austrian envoy Richard Riedl remarked that no government had ever taken office at a harder moment.
entries.source_note: Ullrich, bpb 2023.

entries.headline: Passive resistance in the Ruhr is called off
entries.digest: The Stresemann government ended passive resistance in the Ruhr, admitting that the Reich could no longer pay for it. By the end of September the dollar stood at about 160 million marks.
entries.source_note: Ullrich, bpb 2023 (date and month-end rate). Smithsonian (2023) gives 98.9 million as a September figure, probably an average.

entries.headline: Decree founding the Deutsche Rentenbank
entries.digest: After the coalition agreed in mid-October to create a new bank of issue, the Reich decreed the founding of the Deutsche Rentenbank. The bank's capital was a mortgage charged on German agricultural, industrial and commercial property, because the Reich lacked gold. The new money would rest on a claim on land, and on the public's willingness to accept it.
entries.source_note: Mid-October coalition decision: Ullrich, bpb 2023; mortgage basis: DHM LeMO. The exact decree date of 15 October is the standard reference date but was not checked against the Reichsgesetzblatt itself.

entries.headline: Postage 15 million today, 30 million in two days
entries.digest: Betty Scholem told her son in Palestine that a letter stamp cost 15 million marks and would double within two days. A loaf cost 540 million and a tram ride 20 million. The family printing firm bought dollars to protect its payroll while the staff demanded twice their eight billion. She expected the Rhineland and Ruhr to be lost, Bavaria to break away and Germany to split into small states.
entries.source_note: Mutter und Sohn im Briefwechsel (1989), pp. 84–89; A Life in Letters (2002), pp. 125–27; GHDI.

entries.headline: Germany collapsing step by step
entries.digest: Klemperer wrote that Germany was falling apart slowly and steadily. The dollar was rising by about 300 million marks a day, and the inflation was hitting his household directly. He wondered how long they would have food and where they would have to cut back.
entries.source_note: Quoted in Evans, The Coming of the Third Reich (2003), p. 107, via Facing History; month only.

entries.headline: Peter's anniversary, and no quiet to remember him
entries.digest: On the ninth anniversary of her son Peter's death in the war, Kollwitz wrote that she was too distracted to remember him calmly. A Rhenish Republic had been proclaimed, the dollar stood at 40 billion, a general strike was announced, and there was hunger and confusion everywhere. She felt weighed down and oppressed.
entries.source_note: Die Tagebücher (1989), pp. 561–63; GHDI translation.

entries.headline: The printers have become bankers
entries.digest: Eight days later, the dollar had gone from 10 to 18.5 to about 40 billion in three days, and bread from 900 million to 5.5 billion. The firm now had 130 workers, but its sons were more bankers than book publishers. Their main work was guarding and moving huge sums of paper marks. Some looting had begun, and she expected worse at any time.
entries.source_note: Same editions; GHDI.

entries.headline: A patchwork of monies, and one test for the new one
entries.digest: The weekly described a transition in which the paper mark had collapsed in the second week of October faster than remedies could follow. Towns and firms issued emergency notes, wholesalers used dollars, and dollar treasury certificates and gold-loan notes in one- and two-dollar sizes circulated. The paper mark stayed legal tender. The writer said the key test was whether industry and the public would accept the coming Rentenmark at its gold face value, as the Reich Association of German Industry had agreed to do.
entries.source_note: Wirtschaftsdienst no. 44, 2 November 1923, pp. 1005–1006 (digitised PDF).

entries.headline: Schacht is made Currency Commissioner
entries.digest: Finance Minister Hans Luther asked Schacht to serve as Reich Currency Commissioner, in charge of stabilisation and the Rentenmark. Writing four years later, Schacht stressed the scope of the post: a consultative seat in cabinet and a co-signature on every Reich measure touching the currency.
entries.quote: These, it is true, were no ordinary powers.
entries.source_note: The Stabilization of the Mark (New York: Adelphi, 1927), pp. 90–93; GHDI. Some references give 13 November for the formal appointment.

entries.headline: The dollar passes a trillion marks
entries.digest: For the first time the dollar was quoted above one trillion paper marks (German: eine Billion). Six days earlier, Hitler's putsch in Munich had failed on 8–9 November, and in Berlin unemployment and looting were spreading.
entries.source_note: Ullrich, bpb 2023.

entries.headline: The Rentenmark is issued; the presses stop
entries.digest: The Rentenbank began putting Rentenmark notes into circulation alongside the paper mark, while the Reichsbank stopped discounting Reich Treasury bills, the channel through which the government had been printing money. The dollar was quoted at 2.52 trillion that day. The new notes carried no gold promise, and their backing was the land mortgage and a strict limit on how many would be issued.
entries.source_note: Issue date: DHM LeMO; 2.52 trillion: Ullrich, bpb 2023; end of monetising Reich debt: Mises Institute (2023).

entries.headline: One Rentenmark equals one trillion paper marks
entries.digest: The paper mark was fixed at 4.2 trillion to the dollar, so that one trillion paper marks equalled one Rentenmark, and the Rentenmark stood at 4.20 to the dollar. That was the 1914 rate, a deliberate return to a figure people remembered. The conversion was declared rather than earned, and it held because the issue stopped and people chose to trust the new unit.
entries.source_note: Ullrich, bpb 2023; DHM LeMO; Mises Institute (2023).

entries.headline: The Reichsbank president dies on the day of the fix
entries.digest: Rudolf Havenstein, Reichsbank president since 1908 and appointed for life, died suddenly of a heart attack on the day the rate was fixed. He had presided over the printing of the inflation years. His death cleared the way for Schacht's appointment to the Reichsbank in December.
entries.source_note: Mises Institute (2023) gives 20 November; GHDI's abstract to Schacht's text says 'end of November'.

entries.headline: A toddler asks how the dollar is doing
entries.digest: Kollwitz recorded two small scenes. Her grandson Peter, about two years old, asked his mother how the dollar was. On a tram a six-year-old pointed at the telegraph wires and took them to be 'the dollar'. Children had picked up the exchange rate as part of how they saw the world.
entries.source_note: Die Tagebücher (1989); GHDI translation; dated only 'November 1923'.

entries.headline: Bread at 140 billion, looting, and talk of emigrating
entries.digest: Kollwitz wrote that things were getting worse: looting, attempted pogroms, a rumour that Bavaria was at war with the north. A loaf had cost 140 billion marks and then 80 billion. Her cousin was out of work, a family friend had been dismissed, and the streets were full of unemployed people. Her son Hans and his wife Ottilie talked of emigrating, because a happy life could not be built here.
entries.source_note: Die Tagebücher (1989), pp. 561–63; GHDI. The 'attempted pogroms' refer to events such as the attack on the Scheunenviertel on 5 November 1923 (Ullrich).

entries.headline: A first ray of hope: shoppers return to the food shops
entries.digest: Three weeks after the Rentenmark, Kessler saw cheerful crowds buying in the food shops again and wrote of a first ray of hope breaking through the dark. In his diary, at least, the new money had begun to work.
entries.source_note: Quoted (German) by Ullrich, bpb 2023, as early December 1923.

entries.headline: Schacht becomes Reichsbank president
entries.digest: President Ebert appointed Schacht president of the Reichsbank, against the wishes of the bank's own board. The currency commissioner who had defended the Rentenmark now ran the institution whose printing he had stopped.
entries.source_note: Weimarer Republik e.V. timeline, December 1923; GHDI abstract (board's objection).

entries.headline: The crisis year ends; Germany stood near the abyss
entries.digest: D'Abernon closed the year by writing that the year of crisis was over and that Germany had stood close to the abyss. In his own account, the stabilisation and the survival of the republic were achievements that could easily have failed.
entries.source_note: An Ambassador of Peace, vol. II (1929), quoted (German) by Ullrich, bpb 2023.

entries.headline: Shares, cash and insurance nearly worthless; fear as a Jew
entries.digest: Klemperer recorded that his shares, cash and life insurance were close to worthless and that money worries were wearing at his nerves. As the autumn turned violent he also wrote of fearing for his safety as a Jew. His savings were lost for good, even after the currency was made stable.
entries.source_note: Leben sammeln (1996), as summarised by Smithsonian Magazine (2023); entry dates not given.

entries.headline: Her father's mind changes
entries.digest: What struck her most was the change in her father, a respected merchant. In the years after the inflation he took up a slogan that divided capital into 'creative' German capital and 'parasitic' Jewish capital. She told a friend that one should have known him as he used to be. Her memory shows how financial ruin could turn into a new and false picture of the world.
entries.form: memoir (as told to Pearl S. Buck, 1947)
entries.source_note: Buck, How It Happens (1947), via Financial History 142 (2022), p. 36. The slogan is paraphrased, not repeated.

entries.headline: The Reichsmark replaces the stopgap
entries.digest: Under the Dawes Plan's settlement, the Reichsmark was created as Germany's permanent gold-linked currency, at par with the Rentenmark. The emergency currency of November 1923 had done its work as a temporary measure people agreed to trust.
entries.source_note: DHM LeMO, Währungsreform 1923.

convergences.label: Autumn 1922: the exchange rate becomes the news
convergences.note: Hemingway saw the rate printed in big type and turned it into cheap lunches for foreigners. Weeks later Kessler read the same number as a fever chart, while the official quotation crossed 9,000. To the visitor it meant bargains, and to the resident it meant decline.

convergences.label: After the Ruhr: unity and hunger in the same weeks
convergences.note: D'Abernon saw class hatred give way to patriotism under occupation. In the same weeks Wolfgang counted pensioners dying in his building. The resistance that united the country was paid for in money that was ruining it.

convergences.label: 15 October 1923: a decree and a letter
convergences.note: On the day the new bank was decreed, Betty Scholem was paying 15 million for a stamp and guarding her payroll in dollars. The decree did nothing yet for her prices. It was a promise, and her letter shows why people were slow to trust promises.

convergences.label: 22–23 October 1923: the dollar at 40 billion
convergences.note: Kollwitz and Betty Scholem, a day apart in Berlin, both give the dollar at about 40 billion. One writes about grief she has no quiet to feel, the other about printers turned into money-guards. In Dresden, Klemperer was counting how long the food would last.

convergences.label: Early November 1923: improvised money and street violence
convergences.note: The Hamburg weekly listed emergency notes and dollar certificates and asked whether the new unit would be accepted. In Berlin, within days, hunger became looting and the Scheunenviertel attack that Kollwitz recorded as attempted pogroms. The economists describe the money, and the diarist describes the streets.

convergences.label: 12–20 November 1923: the new agreement is made
convergences.note: Within eight days a commissioner was given exceptional powers, the presses stopped, the Rentenmark was issued, the rate was fixed and the Reichsbank president died. Kollwitz's late-November bread prices, 140 billion and then 80 billion, are the first sign in a diary that the fixed rate was holding.

convergences.label: December 1923: relief, and the cost counted
convergences.note: Kessler saw the food shops full again, and D'Abernon wrote that Germany had come close to the abyss. Klemperer's savings and insurance, like millions of others', did not return. The new money was stable, but the old money was gone.

ties.note: Schacht sat with the cabinet as Currency Commissioner from 12 November and co-signed its currency measures; the official sequence of 15–20 November is the policy he defended.

The British Embassy and the Finance Ministry both stood in Berlin's Wilhelmstraße government quarter. D'Abernon's 1926 Royal Statistical Society paper analysed the same collapse and recovery that Schacht described from the inside in 1927.

Both turned mark prices into North American money. For Hemingway's Toronto readers that meant cheap meals; for Wolfgang, earning in marks, it meant a cheque worth a third of its face value and neighbours starving.
Both in Berlin, a day apart in October 1923, give the dollar at about 40 billion; both record looting and fear of worse.

Two Berlin diarists of the art world in the same city and months, one writing from a poor northern district and the other from a well-off western one. Each read the dollar rate as a sign of the nation's sickness.
Von Pustau remembered the scapegoating of Jews spreading through her Hamburg circle; Klemperer, of Jewish birth, recorded fearing for his safety as the crisis turned violent.
The Hamburg weekly analysed the Reich's planned Rentenmark before its issue, naming acceptance at face value as the test the official measures would have to pass.
Both Berliners record the deaths and hunger of the old and the poor: Wolfgang's pensioners in early 1923, Kollwitz's unemployed streets at the year's end.

threads_out.note: The hyperinflation erased mark-denominated debts and savings by currency collapse rather than by any decree of release. It was an unplanned clean slate, and creditors and savers bore the loss.
The Rentenmark had no gold behind it, only a mortgage, a limit on issue and public confidence. In 1971 the dollar's link to gold was cut, and confidence became its only backing as well.
The reparations set at the peace conference, and the French and Belgian move into the Ruhr to enforce them in January 1923, were the immediate background to the final collapse of the mark.
Betty Scholem's October 1923 letters went to her son Gershom, who had just settled in Jerusalem, where he would become a leading scholar of Jewish mysticism.

Contemporaries and later writers such as Haffner and Zweig argued over how far the ruin of 1923 prepared Germans for the dictatorship that followed. Schacht, who stabilised the mark, later served as Hitler's Reichsbank president.
